:::{#exm-moore-penrose-generalized-inverse}
#### The Moore-Penrose inverse of a rank-one matrix

The $3 \times 2$ matrix $\matr{A}$ below has rank $1$, because its second column is twice its first,
so it has no ordinary inverse.
The function `MASS::ginv()` computes its Moore-Penrose inverse $\matr{G}$.
The code checks the four conditions of @def-moore-penrose,
of which the first is the equation that makes $\matr{G}$ a generalized inverse.

```{r}
#| label: moore-penrose-generalized-inverse
#| code-fold: false
A <- cbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(2, 4, 6))
G <- MASS::ginv(A)
conditions <- c(
  "1: AGA = A" = isTRUE(all.equal(A %*% G %*% A, A)),
  "2: GAG = G" = isTRUE(all.equal(G %*% A %*% G, G)),
  "3: AG symmetric" = isTRUE(all.equal(A %*% G, t(A %*% G))),
  "4: GA symmetric" = isTRUE(all.equal(G %*% A, t(G %*% A)))
)
conditions
round(G, 4)
```

All `{r} sum(conditions)` of `{r} length(conditions)` conditions hold,
so $\matr{G}$ is a Moore-Penrose inverse of $\matr{A}$.
By @thm-moore-penrose-generalized-inverse it is also a generalized inverse,
which is condition 1: $\matr{A}\matr{G}\matr{A} = \matr{A}$ up to rounding error.

:::
